head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Coordinate compression: map the prices to ranks 1..m so they can index an array
Prices are large, but only their ORDER matters
A tree over ranks that supports `update(i, v)` (raise position `i` to at least `v`) and `query(i)` (maximum over positions 1..i) in O(log m)
`i & -i` isolates the lowest set bit; adding it climbs to the next tree node that covers `i`, subtracting it walks down the prefix
Best profit among earlier items with a STRICTLY smaller price: `query(rank − 1)`
The best first element of a triplet ending at `j`
second pass from the right with `m - rank + 1`
Reverse the ranks so that 'larger price to the right' becomes a prefix query again
Mirror trick: one tree type for both directions
Both neighbours must exist (profits are positive, −1 means none)

p: `prices = [10,2,3,4]`, `profits = [100,2,7,10]`. For each middle element `j`: best left profit (smaller price earlier), best right profit (larger price later):
The only valid triplet is the prices `2 < 3 < 4`, with profits 2 + 7 + 10 = 19. The item with price 10 has no larger price after it, so it cannot be a start.

For each middle element we need the maximum profit among earlier elements with a smaller price. Brute force is O(n²); a sorted structure with prefix maximum answers it in O(log n). A Fenwick tree is the compact way to maintain prefix maxima, since values only ever increase.

head: Approach
Time
rows: for each middle scan both sides

2921.takeaway: Maximum profit triplet with increasing prices: for each middle element, take the best smaller-price element to the left and larger-price element to the right, using Fenwick-tree prefix maxima over compressed prices.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Group each person's access times in minutes after midnight (the string `HHMM` is sliced into hours and minutes)
Convert clock strings to numbers; `defaultdict(list)` groups them
The input is not ordered, so sort each person's times
Three consecutive accesses within less than 60 minutes (strictly less: exactly 60 does not count)
Stop at the first qualifying window

p: Accesses `a`: 0549, 0532, 0621; `b`: 0457, 0540 (minutes after midnight):

In sorted order, any three accesses inside a 60-minute span include three consecutive ones, and the tightest span for a trio starting at `i` is `ts[i]` to `ts[i + 2]`. If that is not under 60, no other trio starting at `i` can be.

2933.takeaway: High-access employees: convert times to minutes, sort per person, and flag anyone with three consecutive accesses less than 60 minutes apart.

head: Code
Meaning

rows: Keep the bits of `a` ABOVE position `n` unchanged (they are not affected by `x < 2ⁿ`)
Decide the n free bits from the most significant to the least
The XOR (exclusive OR) with `x` can flip each of these bits freely
If the two bits are equal, choosing `x` to make BOTH 1 is best (both numbers grow)
Equal bits: `x` bit = complement of both
If they differ, exactly one of the results gets a 1: give it to the SMALLER number
The sum `ca + cb` is fixed once bits are chosen; the product is largest when the two are as close as possible

head: Bit

Decision

rows: bits differ: give the 1 to the smaller number
bits differ: give the 1 to the smaller number

p: The final numbers are 14 and 7, product 98. A brute force over all `x < 2⁴` gives the same maximum.

blocks.h: Why give the extra 1 to the smaller number?
p: For two numbers with a fixed sum, the product is largest when they are closest. Where the bits differ, XOR with `x` decides which number gets the 1, and the sum of the two numbers at that bit is the same either way. Giving it to the smaller number keeps them close. Where bits agree, making both 1 raises the sum, which is always better.

2939.takeaway: Maximum XOR product: bits above n are fixed; from high to low, make equal bits both 1, and give a differing bit's 1 to the currently smaller number to keep the product large.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Prefix sums, so the sum of any block `j+1..i` is `pre[i] - pre[j]`
Most blocks into which the first `i` elements can be merged so that block sums are non-decreasing
The SUM of the final block in that best split (keeping it as small as possible)
The next block must be at least this big
The block after `j` must not be smaller than the block before it
`dp` never decreases as the prefix grows, and a later `j` also makes the last block smaller; so take the largest valid `j`

Keeps candidates ordered by the key `pre[j] + last[j]` (increasing); pop from the front while the NEXT candidate is also valid, and pop from the back candidates with a key not smaller than the new one
Sliding-window style optimisation: O(1) amortised instead of a scan

p: `nums = [4,3,2,6]` → prefix sums `[0,4,7,9,15]`. For each prefix length `i`, the chosen previous cut `j`:
`dp[4] = 3`: for example `[4]`, `[3+2]`, `[6]` has block sums 4, 5, 6, which is non-decreasing. A brute force over all splits agrees on random inputs.

For each `i` we need the largest `j` with `pre[j] + last[j] <= pre[i]`. As `i` grows, `pre[i]` only grows, so a candidate that is valid stays valid, and candidates with a larger key that sit before candidates with a smaller key are useless. A deque keeps candidates in increasing key order, so the valid ones are at the front and each index is pushed and popped once.

2945.takeaway: Maximum non-decreasing array length after merging subarrays: DP over prefixes with the previous block's sum, using a monotonic deque to find the best previous cut in O(1) amortised.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Indices ordered by value (an index sort)
Neighbours in sorted order that differ by at most `limit` can be swapped, and swapping is transitive through chains
Build groups (connected components) by scanning the sorted values
Each group is a set of indices whose values can be freely rearranged among those positions
Elements in one group can reach each other's positions through swaps
`sorted(g)` and `vals = sorted(nums[i] for i in g)`
Positions in increasing order and the group's values in increasing order
Smallest array: put the smallest value at the smallest position
Write the sorted values into the sorted positions

p: `nums = [1,5,3,9,8]`, `limit = 2`: sorted values 1, 3, 5, 8, 9 split into the groups `{1,3,5}` and `{8,9}` (gaps 2, 2, 3, 1).

blocks.h: Why can a group be sorted freely?
p: Two values within `limit` can swap directly. If `a` and `b` can swap and `b` and `c` can swap, then `a` can reach `c` (swap through `b`), so every value in a chain of close values can be moved to any other position of the chain. Sorting the values of a group into the group's positions gives the lexicographically smallest arrangement.

head: Approach
Time
rows: sort and cut at big gaps (this code)

2948.takeaway: Smallest array by swaps within a limit: sort the values, cut into groups wherever consecutive values differ by more than the limit, and sort each group into its own positions.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Healthy children before the first sick one and after the last: each such end gap is infected in ONE direction only
End gaps have a forced order
Healthy children between two consecutive sick ones: infection can come from both sides
Middle gaps have a choice at every step except the last
Total number of healthy children to infect
Orderings of all `m` children if there were no ordering constraints
`* pow(factorial(g), MOD - 2, MOD)` for each gap
Divide by `g!` for each gap, because inside a gap the order is NOT free (see below): this removes the over-counted arrangements
Modular division uses the modular inverse (Fermat's little theorem, MOD is prime)
`* pow(2, g - 1, MOD)` for each middle gap
Inside a middle gap of size `g` there are `2^(g−1)` orders: each infection can extend from the left or the right end, except the last child, which is forced

p: `n = 5`, `sick = [0, 4]`: no end gaps, one middle gap of size 3, `m = 3` healthy children.

blocks.h: Why do the gaps interleave freely but have internal order?
p: Different gaps are independent: an infection in one gap never affects another, so the `m` children can be ordered by choosing which positions of the sequence belong to which gap (a multinomial coefficient `m! / ∏ g!`). Within one gap, though, the order is constrained: an end gap must be infected from the sick side outward (1 way), and a middle gap can grow from either end, giving `2^(g−1)` orders.

For `n = 4`, `sick = [1]`, there is one end gap of 1 (before) and one of 2 (after): `3!/(1!·2!) = 3` sequences, the code returns 3. The code was also checked against a brute-force simulation on random small inputs.

bullets: Time: O(n) for the factorials (each `pow` is O(log MOD)).

2954.takeaway: Infection sequences: interleave the independent gaps with a multinomial (m! over the gap factorials) and multiply 2^(g−1) for each gap with sick children on both sides.

Change `word[i]` to a letter that differs from both neighbours (always possible with 26 letters); that also removes any conflict between `word[i]` and `word[i+1]`, so skip one extra position
Greedy: one change fixes two adjacent pairs
The pair is fine; move on

blocks.h: Why is the greedy skip correct?
p: When `word[i]` conflicts with `word[i − 1]`, changing `word[i]` to a letter far from both neighbours fixes this pair AND the next pair `(word[i], word[i+1])`. So any problem involving the next position disappears, and the scan resumes at `i + 2`. Fixing the left letter instead would leave the conflict with the right neighbour possibly alive.

2957.takeaway: Remove almost-equal adjacent characters: scan left to right; on a conflict change the right letter to something far away and skip the next position.

The whole array is already strictly increasing: every subarray (all `n(n+1)/2` of them) can be removed
Removals that keep only a prefix of the array: remove `nums[l..n-1]` for any `l` from 0 to `i + 1` (keeping `0..i+1` elements, the empty prefix included), which is `i + 2` choices
Count removals that keep only a prefix

Two pointers over the prefix and suffix

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: The extra street is parallel to an existing one, so the graph is just a path: distance `k` has `n − k` unordered pairs
After the extra street, houses `x..y` form a CYCLE of `m` houses; `a` houses form a tail hanging off `x`, `b` houses a tail hanging off `y`
Split the graph into a cycle and two paths
A difference array: add `v` to every distance in `l..r` in O(1)
Range updates, prefix sum at the end
`add(1, half, m)` (+ the `m // 2` term for even `m`)
Pairs of cycle houses: for each distance `1..⌊(m−1)/2⌋` there are `m` unordered pairs, and for even `m` exactly `m/2` pairs at distance `m/2`
`for tail in (a, b): for s in 1..tail`

A tail house `s` steps from the cycle reaches the attachment house at distance `s`, the next `half` cycle houses on both sides at `s+1..s+half` (two of each), and for even `m` the opposite house at `s + m/2`
A left-tail house `s` and a right-tail house `t` are `s + 1 + t` apart through the extra street
Pairs of houses on the SAME tail at distance `d` (a path)

p: `n = 5`, `x = 2`, `y = 4`: the cycle has `m = 3` houses, the left tail `a = 1` and the right tail `b = 1`. The result for distances 1..5 is [10, 8, 2, 0, 0].

blocks.h: Why split into cycle and tails?
p: Distances inside a cycle depend only on the cyclic distance (the smaller of the two ways around), and distances from a tail house to anything follow from its distance to the cycle plus distances inside the cycle. Each category contributes a simple range of distances, which the difference array adds in O(1). The formula was checked against a breadth-first search on every `(n, x, y)` with `n ≤ 12`.

3017.takeaway: Houses at each distance with one extra street: split into a cycle and two tails, add each category's distance range with a difference array, and double for ordered pairs.

head: Code
Meaning
Reach for it when
rows: Letter counts over ALL words: operations let us swap any two characters, so only the pooled multiset matters
Swaps anywhere make the letters a shared pool
Number of matched letter pairs available; a palindrome of length `L` needs `L // 2` pairs (a middle letter, if any, can be any leftover letter)
Palindromes are made of mirrored pairs
Shortest words first: they cost the fewest pairs
Greedy: build as many palindromes as possible
Not enough pairs for the next (and every longer) word
Spend the pairs and count one more palindromic word

p: `words = ["abbb","ba","aa"]`: pooled letters {'a': 4, 'b': 4}, so there are 3 pairs (`a·a`, `b·b`, and one more `b·b`).

blocks.h: Why is the middle letter free?
p: An odd-length palindrome needs one unpaired middle letter. A leftover single letter from the pool serves, and odd-length words have as many middles available as there are words, since every leftover letter appears in the pool. Only the pairs are a limiting resource.

bullets: Time: O(total length + w log w).

3035.takeaway: Maximum palindromic words after swaps: pool all letters, count mirrored pairs, and spend them on the shortest words first.
